issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette:
Evan Collins was a 34-year-old Navy officer who came to treatment after months of trying to manage on his own. He grew up in the United States and had built a life that, until recently, had felt orderly and purposeful: long hours on base, a stable marriage, regular contact with friends from work and from home. That changed after a natural disaster struck while he was away with his unit. In the aftermath, he found himself in a chaotic, crowded scene where the usual sense of structure and control had vanished. He remembered the event afterward less as a continuous story than as a sequence of images: the physical setting, the press of people around him, and brief snapshots of fear that did not fit together into something that felt fully real. When he tried to describe it, he often said it was hard to believe it had actually happened to him, as if he were recounting something that belonged to someone else.

In the early weeks after the disaster, Evan noticed that certain places brought the experience back with unusual force. Crowded places were especially difficult. A packed store aisle, a busy lunch line on base, or a tightly filled room could make him feel hemmed in and on edge, with the same urgent discomfort he had felt when too many people were packed together during the disaster. Physical locations also carried weight. He became wary of settings that reminded him of the event, especially places that felt enclosed, exposed, or strangely similar in atmosphere to where things had gone wrong. Even at home, being in the dark could unsettle him, because the combination of darkness and uncertainty evoked the conditions of the frightening event. He also became acutely aware of alcohol smell. If he caught it on someone’s breath or lingering in a social setting, he would feel a sharp, immediate tightening, as though the present scene had suddenly been linked to the past.

His memories of the disaster came to him mostly as pictures. He would see fragments rather than a full narrative, and when that happened he felt something almost bodily about it. He described it as if his body were back in the same position it had been in during the event, with the same physical helplessness and strain. The memory did not unfold as a clear verbal account, and that made it feel even more extreme to him, almost unbelievable, like a scene too intense to belong to his own life. At times he would stop mid-sentence, stare ahead, and seem to sense the event in his body before he could organize it into words.

Over the months that followed, Evan began to pull back from the parts of life that once anchored him. He avoided seeing friends, turning down invitations and gradually letting conversations lapse. He also stayed away from situations that reminded him of the disaster, especially darkness and crowded environments, which meant changing routines around errands, social plans, and even the way he moved through familiar spaces. On some evenings at home he would keep lights on longer than others preferred, not because he expected anything to happen, but because being in the dark felt too close to the conditions of the event. At work, he managed to keep functioning, but he noticed that the easiest way to get through the day was to stay busy and keep interactions brief. Over time, the distance from friends and the narrowing of his routine left him feeling increasingly cut off from the people around him.

Evan’s thoughts about himself became harsher as the months passed. He told himself he deserved to suffer because of what happened, even though he struggled to explain what that meant in any concrete sense. He had once thought of himself as a happy person, but now he saw himself as miserable most of the time. He felt that he no longer belonged anywhere, neither fully with his Navy peers nor fully in the ordinary life he shared with his wife. At gatherings, even when he was physically present, he felt isolated and set apart, as if everyone else occupied a world to which he no longer had access. That sense of distance was especially painful because it contrasted so sharply with the kind of man he believed he had been before the disaster.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become difficult to ignore. He was still meeting the demands of his job as a Navy officer, but the effort of moving through crowded spaces, avoiding reminders, and keeping social distance had started to shape nearly every part of his week. What brought him in was not a single collapse but the accumulation of these changes and the fear that he was becoming permanently disconnected from the life he had known. He hoped treatment might help him make sense of the event without being flooded by images and bodily reactions, and he was most afraid that the sense of being isolated, miserable, and out of place might never lift.
